title: Plato, Hobbes, Mill, and the never-ending fight against inequality
subtitle: Three philosophers on the wealth gap
author: David Lay Williams
introduction: The growing gap between the rich and the poor is a problem that seems increasingly urgent with each passing day. From the shocking statistics about wealth concentration in the United States and Britain to the widespread struggle for basic needs like food, the signs of economic inequality are impossible to ignore. Yet, what many overlook is that inequality is not a new phenomenon—it's been a persistent feature of human societies for millennia. From ancient philosophers like Plato to modern thinkers such as John Stuart Mill, a long line of intellectuals have not only chronicled the rise of inequality but also warned of its devastating consequences. Professor David Lay Williams argues the answers to inequality may have surprising insights from the past.
body:
New statistics seem to appear every day with sobering news about growing levels of economic inequality.  Recently, the Congressional Budget Office in the United States reported that American families in the top 10 percent now hold 60 percent of all national wealth, with the bottom 50 percent holding 6 percent of national wealth.  In Britain, the top 20 percent of households possess 63 percent of all national wealth.  Meanwhile, the BBC reports that a record 9.3 million people in Britain are struggling with putting food on the table.  And if the data are accurate, the trends suggest further accentuating the gap between rich and poor.

Naturally, inequality and its dramatic growth over the past few decades have drawn attention from journalists, activists, scholars, and politicians.  Thomas Piketty’s Capital in the Twenty-First Century tracked inequality’s trends over the past few centuries, observing how it peaked in the Gilded Age, diminished in the aftermath of the Second World War, and then started rising again during the Thatcher and Reagan administrations respectively, continuing largely unabated since then.

As long as inequality has persisted, people have observed it, chronicled the challenges it raises, and suggested reforms for reducing it in order to mitigate those challenges.

To the extent most have thought about the matter, that may be as much as they know.  Yet inequality has largely predominated for much of recorded history.  The Stanford University historian, Walter Scheidel, has observed in his Great Leveler that “Inequality either grew or held fairly steady for much of recorded history.”  A generation earlier, the Yale political scientist, Charles Lindbloom, similarly remarked, “Historically, all societies, market or not, have preserved economic inequality.”  Indeed, inequality has a very long history.

But what is less well known among many contemporary economists, social activists, and political figures, however, is that as long as inequality has persisted, people have observed it, chronicled the challenges it raises, and suggested reforms for reducing it in order to mitigate those challenges. Careful attention to this long tradition can help enrich our understanding of inequality and stimulate more creative thinking about potential solutions.

Indeed, it will be surprising to some that among the greatest critics of inequality was none other than the ancient Athenian philosopher, Plato.  I say this is surprising because Plato is often considered an inegalitarian philosopher, insofar as in his celebrated Republic, Socrates advises that all political power be given to a small handful of philosophers, who rule without checks or oversight of any kind.  But even in this inegalitarian doctrine, Plato’s concern about the effects of money on politics is evident – insofar as those rulers are not allowed to have any property or personal wealth whatsoever.  In fact, they are not even allowed to be under the same roof as precious metal, such as gold and silver.  Philosophers are only to be entrusted insofar as they are not subjected the temptations of enriching themselves.

But it is not only the philosophers that concern Plato in his Republic. He is concerned about the effects of concentrated wealth and inequality on the city more generally. While private citizens are allowed to have private property, no one should have too much or too little of it, since great inequality results in dividing a single city into two parallel cities – one of the rich and one of the poor.

SUGGESTED READING Hobbes vs Rousseau: are we inherently evil? By Robin Douglass

Plato’s concern about inequality is even more explicit in his final dialogue, The Laws, which goes so far as to observe that great inequality inevitably brings about what he calls “the greatest of all plagues,” namely, civil war, which he views as the inevitable result of excessive inequality. To this extent, his character of the Athenian Stranger counsels that in an ideal state that the richest households should have no more than four times the wealth and property of the poorest. Those with more will have their surpluses taxed and drawn back to the state for public uses or redistribution.

Of course, Plato was only the first of the great Western philosophers to express concern about inequality. Many others, including many of the best known among them, such as Aristotle, Thomas Hobbes, Jean-Jacques Rousseau, Adam Smith, John Stuart Mill, and Karl Marx, have argued along similar lines.

Hobbes is an illustrative example. Born in early modern England, he observed the rise of the merchant class and its wealth. As this class grew richer and sought corresponding political authority in the House of Commons, of course, Parliament grew increasingly estranged from the Crown ultimately resulting in the English Civil War, which Hobbes associated with the rise of new forms of concentrated wealth.  The wealthy merchants’ refusal to pay their ship money taxes was a direct result of their growing “presumption of impunity” – people as rich as them were simply above moral and legal norms.

It was for this reason that he wrote in his Leviathan, that the commonwealth is radically endangered when its treasury “is gathered in too much abundance in one or a few private men.”  Hobbes’s solution was to authorize the sovereign to confiscate and redistribute property according to “equity and the common good,” namely to safeguard the peace.  It is only through a degree of economic equality that sustained peace, for him, is possible.

SUGGESTED READING Nietzsche's unwitting case for equality By Donovan Miyasaki

John Stuart Mill is yet another instructive example.  Most famous today for his defense of liberty, the Victorian philosopher was also deeply troubled by inequality.  Responding to Tocqueville’s observations about America’s relative equality, Mill lamented that in Britain, “Great fortunes are continually accumulated, and seldom redistributed.”  He lamented this because of inequality’s moral and social effects.  Morally, he worried that inequality incentivized a corrupting unnatural selfishness that consumed the rich.  It would lead them, among other things, to seek large profits at any costs, including by fraud, which happened regularly with adulterated foods in the nineteenth century.  This drive to profit would often come with moral and physical costs to the poorest citizens.

But Mill was especially concerned with the social and political effects of inequality on Britain.  Great inequality pitted the classes against one another, creating a “concealed enmity . . . [and] soured animosity which is universal in this country towards the whole class of employers, in the class of the employed.”  As Mill also observed, this hostility resulted in a “total absence of regard for justice and fairness” among both classes when dealing with the other – a condition that would continue to long as the classes felt the other harbored “interests and feelings [that] are in hostility” to the other.

Beyond this, Mill worried obsessively about the dangers of what he called “class legislation,” namely the seizing of political power by the ascendent class to convert its interests into laws for the entire nation.  As he observed in his Rationale of Representation, “In every country where there are rich and poor, the administration of public affairs would, even under the most democratic constitution, be mainly in the hands of the rich; as has been the case in all the republics of the old world, ancient and modern.”

While selfishness might encourage the growth of industry, it never knows where to stop and when it has crossed very serious moral boundaries in exploiting the poor.

Mill offered myriad solutions to mitigate the inequality fuelling these troubles.  Perhaps most notably among them was his proposal of a steep inheritance tax, which would cap fortunes at what anyone one person could earn in a single lifetime, rather than letting those inequalities grow over generations.  But more than that, Mill advocated for worker co-ops, where corporations would be owned by the people working in them – which, he argued, would naturally curtail inflated executive salaries.  He also entertained reversing the effects of the enclosure laws by granting several acres to all citizens to farm their own lands without becoming dependent on wealthy employers.

But perhaps most notable among Mill’s many reforms is the most modest: educational reforms directly at unlearning the profound selfishness that had taken full root by the Industrial Age.  Unlike Bentham, and more like Marx, Mill regarded selfishness as unnatural and detrimental to civilization.  While selfishness might encourage the growth of industry, it never knows where to stop and when it has crossed very serious moral boundaries in exploiting the poor.  Mill thinks human nature is more inclined to seek community with one’s neighbors than to exploit them.  But rampant capitalism has dampened this instinct in favor of the profit motive.  So Mill argued that schools needed to begin teaching the evils of unchecked selfishness and the natural sentiments of community.  Such a reform, though modest in comparison to inheritance taxes and reverse enclosure laws, would have far-reaching effects on inequality and social life more generally.

Of course, there are others among the most important Western thinkers who are already well-known for their opposition to inequality, such as Rousseau and Marx.  But it is important to understand that Rousseau and Marx are not outliers in this tradition.  Their opposition to inequality is actually the tradition itself.  Far rarer in the tradition is to find serious and principled defences of inequality.

Inequality is greater now than it has been any time since the Gilded Age.

This survey across a few thinkers is enough to suggest that criticisms of inequality today are not to be dismissed out of hand as the politics of “envy” or “class war.”  Opposition to inequality as it may be found in today’s discourse is merely the latest manifestation of a long tradition.

Inequality is greater now than it has been any time since the Gilded Age.  And a recent Pew poll suggests that inequality concerns citizens across the globe now more than ever. Those tempted to dismiss this yawning gap would do well to consider the long history of concern about inequality and its effects on social and political life.  To dismiss inequality’s dangers is effectively to dismiss much of the accumulated wisdom of the past.  And for those who agree with this tradition’s concerns about inequality, they would similarly do well to consult it for enhanced confidence in calling out its injustices, as well as a resource to stimulate its imagination for confronting and reversing existing trends before they bring the classes to the point of conflict, or what Plato, again, called the “greatest of all plagues.”  We are hardly the first to confront inequality – we’d be foolish to ignore the lessons of the past.

David Lay Williams is Professor of Political Science at DePaul University at is the author of The Greatest of All Plagues: How Economic Inequality Shaped Political Thought from Plato to Marx published by Princeton University Press.
